title: Large language models as uncertainty-calibrated optimizers for experimental discovery - Nature Machine Intelligence
gist: EPFL researchers introduce GOLLuM, which fine-tunes LLMs jointly with Gaussian processes on the GP's own marginal-likelihood objective, turning LLM overconfidence into a calibrated training signal so natural-language-described experiments can be optimized as reliably as -- and more sample-efficiently than -- traditional Bayesian optimization: it matches BO with over 40% fewer experiments and nearly doubles high-yield reaction discovery (43% vs 24-25%) across 23 chemistry and materials benchmarks, while showing naive LLM-as-optimizer prompting fails 10-80% of the time due to hallucination.

themes.theme: Core thesis: uncertainty as a training signal

insights.claim: GOLLuM (Gaussian process Optimized LLMs) trains large language models jointly with a Gaussian process through the GP's marginal likelihood, converting the LLM's core weakness -- hallucination and overconfidence -- into a precise, uncertainty-guided learning signal that reorganizes the LLM's embedding space so experiments with similar outcomes cluster together.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A generalizable recipe for making LLMs trustworthy decision-makers in any high-stakes domain requiring calibrated confidence, not just chemistry.
insights.quote: transforming their overconfidence from a fundamental flaw into a precise learning signal

insights.claim: The authors frame their result as pointing to a different paradigm for specializing foundation models: not through more training data, but through richer, uncertainty-guided information during fine-tuning.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Implies vertical/domain LLM specialization for scientific and high-stakes use cases may not require the massive proprietary datasets many startups assume they need -- a lower-capital path to differentiated LLM products.
insights.quote: GOLLuM points to a different paradigm for specializing foundation models: not through more data but through richer, uncertainty-guided information

insights.claim: Across 23 cross-domain optimization tasks spanning organic synthesis, materials science, process chemistry and molecular design, GOLLuM ranked first on average and matched traditional Bayesian optimization's performance while using over 40% fewer experiments.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Fewer physical experiments needed translates directly into faster, cheaper R&D cycles for pharma, battery, catalysis and materials companies where each wet-lab experiment carries real time and cost.
insights.quote: It matches traditional Bayesian optimization with over 40% fewer experiments

insights.claim: On the Buchwald-Hartwig cross-coupling reaction benchmark, GOLLuM nearly doubled the discovery rate of high-performing reaction conditions compared with expert quantum-chemical descriptors and state-of-the-art LLMs, reaching 43% versus 24-25%.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A near-doubling of hit-rate on a standard pharma-relevant coupling reaction is the kind of efficiency gain that could materially compress process-chemistry development timelines.
insights.quote: nearly doubles the discovery of high-performing Buchwald–Hartwig reactions over expert quantum-chemical descriptors and state-of-the-art LLMs (43% versus 24–25%)

insights.claim: Starting from only ten low-performing 'cold start' experiments and a 50-experiment budget, GOLLuM achieved 36.3% top-5% coverage, beating other LLM-Bayesian-optimization baselines BoChemian (26.5%) and LAPEFT (12.1%), and outperforming standard Bayesian optimization with domain-tailored descriptors (29.7%).
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Performs well under realistic early-stage-campaign constraints (minimal starting data), which is the actual condition most experimental programs begin from.
insights.locator: Across the 23 problems, GOLLuM (PLLMϕ + T5) ranks first on average

insights.claim: The largest performance gains occurred in process chemistry, where GOLLuM improved coverage from 13.4% to 25.4%, a 90% relative improvement over traditional Bayesian optimization.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Process/reaction-condition optimization, a core activity for pharma manufacturing and CDMOs, is where this technique shows outsized near-term commercial value.
insights.quote: The largest gains occur in process chemistry, where GOLLuM improves coverage from 13.4% (GP) to 25.4% top-5% with a 90% relative improvement
insights.locator: Performance also exhibits clear domain structure

insights.claim: In molecular property optimization tasks where strong hand-engineered molecular fingerprints already exist, GOLLuM's edge over baselines narrows to a still-positive 47.9-53.2% coverage, indicating the technology's comparative advantage is largest precisely where good domain-specific descriptors do not already exist.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A useful prioritization lens: apply this approach first to novel or under-instrumented material classes lacking mature descriptors, where the uplift is largest.
insights.locator: In molecular property optimization tasks, where established molecular fingerprints already provide strong signal

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf, non-fine-tuned LLM embeddings -- including OpenAI's proprietary embeddings -- discovered only 15-26% of top-yielding reactions in a controlled Buchwald-Hartwig benchmark, trailing the 38% achieved by specialized chemistry reaction fingerprints (DRFP).
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Warns against the common shortcut of feeding raw LLM embeddings straight into a Bayesian optimizer; this systematically underperforms purpose-built chemistry descriptors and should not be assumed to work.
insights.locator: In 50 optimization trials, LLM embeddings helped discover only 15–26% of the highest-yielding reactions

insights.claim: A chemistry-specialized language model (T5Chem) underperforms general-purpose LLMs, reaching only a 23% discovery rate despite extensive chemical pretraining, but switching its input format from a plain-text experimental procedure to SMILES molecular notation improved its discovery rate by 44%, showing input format matters more than domain-specific pretraining.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Cautions against assuming that more domain-specific pretraining automatically improves LLM performance on scientific tasks; representation/format engineering can be the bigger lever, relevant to anyone building vertical scientific LLM products.
insights.quote: Changing T5Chem's input from an experimental procedure to the Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System (SMILES) format improved its discovery rate by 44%
insights.locator: The simple lack of chemical knowledge does not explain these differences

insights.claim: The authors identify a diagnostic metric -- the ratio of the Gaussian process's learned lengthscale to the average pairwise embedding distance -- that predicts whether an embedding space will work well for Bayesian optimization far more strongly (correlation 0.92) than standard regression accuracy metrics like R-squared (correlation 0.78).
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A generalizable diagnostic tool for evaluating whether any learned embedding space (not just chemistry) is suitable for downstream Bayesian optimization, useful for teams building similar pipelines.

themes.theme: Direct LLM prompting fails as a scientific optimizer

insights.claim: When state-of-the-art proprietary and open-weight LLMs were prompted directly to propose next experimental conditions on the Buchwald-Hartwig benchmark, failure rates ranged from 10% to roughly 80%, driven by hallucinated chemical structures, proposals outside the valid parameter space, duplicate suggestions, and unparsable outputs.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: A strong caution against the increasingly common 'just ask an LLM what to try next' approach in labs; any startup selling raw LLM-driven experiment-suggestion tools without uncertainty calibration carries meaningful reliability risk in automated/self-driving lab settings.
insights.locator: A quantitative analysis revealed high failure rates across all tested models (10% to ~80%

insights.claim: Direct LLM-prompted optimization substantially underperformed both traditional Bayesian optimization using density-functional-theory or reaction-fingerprint descriptors and GOLLuM in top-5% coverage, confirming raw LLM reasoning is not yet a reliable substitute for principled probabilistic decision-making in automated experimental workflows.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Reinforces that in regulated, high-stakes, or capital-intensive lab settings, uncertainty-calibrated hybrid methods should be preferred over naive LLM prompting for autonomous decision-making.
insights.locator: direct prompting underperformed, trailing both standard GP methods and GOLLuM

insights.claim: GOLLuM's fine-tuned latent space spontaneously self-organizes according to real chemistry without being explicitly instructed, clustering high-reactivity iodide-based aryl halide reactions in high-yield regions while separating out less-reactive chloride-based reactions.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Provides a human-checkable rationale for AI-suggested experiments before they are run, directly addressing the 'black box' trust problem that limits AI adoption in regulated or high-stakes R&D settings.
insights.locator: automatically clustering iodide-based reagents in high-yield regions while separating low-performing chlorides

insights.claim: Across domains, GOLLuM identifies the high-performing Mn-Na-W region of a catalyst design space in materials science, favorable ether-alcohol solvent systems in process chemistry, and known structure-property trends for organic photoswitches in molecular design, all without any explicit domain instruction.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Suggests genuinely transferable chemical understanding emerges from the training objective itself, reducing the need for per-domain feature engineering when deploying this method to a new chemistry vertical.
insights.locator: in analytic and process chemistry, the model identifies optimal ether-alcohol solvent systems

insights.claim: The joint GP-LLM training approach generalizes across major LLM architecture families: encoder-decoder models (Google T5, 79% relative improvement), decoder-only models (Qwen-7B, 61% relative improvement), encoder-only models (ModernBERT, 42% improvement), and even closed-source API embeddings via a lightweight projection layer (OpenAI, 31% improvement) without requiring access to the underlying model weights.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: The technique is not locked to a single vendor's model and works even on closed-weight API embeddings, lowering switching costs and making it deployable by companies using GPT/Claude-style closed models via a thin add-on layer.
insights.locator: Similar improvements held across other architecture types

insights.claim: The authors flag the cubic computational scaling of standard Gaussian processes as a real constraint for optimization campaigns involving thousands of experiments, and note the method's effectiveness may be reduced in domains lacking clean linguistic structure, such as protein conformations or crystal structures.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Defines the near-term commercial sweet spot as small-to-medium text-describable chemistry campaigns rather than large-scale screening or structural biology, absent further engineering work.
insights.locator: we acknowledge several limitations that open avenues for future research

insights.claim: The work was developed at EPFL's Institute of Chemical Sciences and Engineering (Schwaller group) with funding from Switzerland's NCCR Catalysis; co-author Ryan-Rhys Griffiths is affiliated with QuantumGreen in San Francisco, and the code was released open-source via GitHub and Zenodo.
insights.speaker: Nature Machine Intelligence
insights.so_what: Signals a bridge between academic self-driving-lab research and a commercial/startup context in the AI-for-chemistry space, and open-sourced code lowers the barrier for other teams or startups to adopt or build on the method directly.
